Where it began

Ian Chappell was born in Unley, near Adelaide, on 26 September 1943, the eldest of four boys. Cricket was everywhere. His father, a respected Adelaide grade player, had him holding a bat almost before he was steady on his feet, and his grandfather Vic Richardson had captained Australia. Two of his younger brothers, Greg and Trevor, also played for Australia.

He grew up in Glenelg and went to Prince Alfred College. A fine baseball catcher too, he was twice picked as an All-Australian. At 18 he made his first-class debut for South Australia, early in 1962.

The player

His first Test came against Pakistan at Melbourne in December 1964, but it took him a few years to settle. Moved up to number three in 1968–69, he found his place and his game. He played 75 Tests between 1964 and 1980, scoring 5,345 runs at 42.42 with 14 hundreds, and held 104 catches, most of them at slip. He became the first Australian to reach a hundred Test catches.

He took over as captain in February 1971 and led Australia in 30 Tests, winning 15 and losing only five. The high point was winning back the Ashes 4–1 in 1974–75, and a few months later he took Australia to the first World Cup final, at Lord's. His highest Test score was 196, against Pakistan at Adelaide.

What made him special

He liked to attack, with the bat and with his field placings, and his teams played the same way. His favourite shot was the hook. For a while he gave it up because it kept getting him out, until a talk with Sir Donald Bradman persuaded him to bring it back. He then spent a winter practising it by hitting baseballs his brother Greg threw at him.

The brothers made history together. At the Oval in 1972 they became the first brothers to make hundreds in the same Test innings, and at Wellington in 1973–74 the first to each make a hundred in both innings of one Test. As a bowler, Ian was more of a part-timer: 20 Test wickets at 65.80 suggest his leg-spin was best kept for emergencies.

Away from the middle

Known to everyone as Chappelli, he was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009. He helped start a players' association that later grew into the Australian Cricketers' Association. Two stands at the Adelaide Oval carry the family name, and in 2004 the Chappell–Hadlee Trophy was created in the family's honour.

He became one of the game's best-known voices, commentating on Channel Nine from 1980–81 until 2018 and retiring from radio in August 2022. He has also championed greater recognition for the Aboriginal team that toured England in 1868.

And finally

When the young Chappell made his first first-class hundred, Richie Benaud was puzzled by his habit of gritting his teeth as the bowler ran in. To Benaud it looked as if he were grinning. Given how much he enjoyed batting, perhaps he was.
